steps.body: Chapter 2 showed the statistic wobbling from sample to sample. Now stack those wobbles up: draw sample after sample and pile each proportion on a line. The pile that grows has a shape — and it is always the same shape.
Draw 20 samples and watch the pile.

widget.prompt: Population truth: 50% purple. Draw 20 samples of 50 and stack their proportions.
widget.successFeedback: A mound: tallest at 0.5, thinning symmetrically to both sides. That mound is the sampling distribution taking its bell shape.
widget.wrongSizeFeedback: Use samples of 50 — the bigger sample makes the bell tighter and easier to see.
widget.moreDrawsFeedback: Keep drawing — the shape needs about 20 stacked samples to show itself.

predict.prompt: Twenty sample proportions get stacked on a line. What shape does the pile take?

options.label: A mound — tall in the middle, thin at the edges

predict.reveal: Middling results are common and extreme ones rare, so the pile mounds up over the truth and thins outward — symmetric, single-peaked: a bell. Chance doesn't spread evenly; it clusters.

widget.prompt: Where does the bell sit tallest?

options.label: Over the population's true value
options.feedback: Yes — sample results cluster around what's actually there: 0.5.

options.label: Over zero
options.feedback: The pile centers on the truth, not the origin.

options.label: Somewhere new each time
options.feedback: With enough draws the peak is stable — it parks over 0.5.

widget.successFeedback: The bell centers on the truth. That's why one decent sample is *evidence*: it probably fell near the middle.

steps.body: Read the pile you just built.
explanationVariants: The stacked proportions mound over 0.5 because middling samples are common and extreme ones rare — the peak marks the parameter.
If the peak sat anywhere but the truth, sampling itself would be biased; honest sampling centers the bell on what's really there.

widget.prompt: A sample proportion of 0.42 and one of 0.58 — which is the bell more surprised by?

options.label: Neither — they sit the same distance from 0.5
options.feedback: Symmetry: 0.08 below and 0.08 above are equally rare.

options.label: 0.42 — undershooting is rarer
options.feedback: The bell has no favorite side; equal distances, equal surprise.

options.label: 0.58 — overshooting is rarer
options.feedback: Same distance from center means the same height on the curve.

widget.successFeedback: The bell is symmetric about the truth: distance matters, direction doesn't.

explanationVariants: 0.42 and 0.58 are mirror images across the center: the symmetric bell assigns them identical rarity.
Surprise under the bell is a function of distance from μ alone — direction never enters.
The mound of sample proportions centers on the parameter the samples estimate — with a true 50%, the peak stands at 50.
Each sample wobbles around the truth, high and low in equal measure, so the stack's center IS the truth: 50.

widget.prompt: The true proportion is 50%. The pile of twenty sample proportions peaks at about what percent?

commonErrors.feedback: That counts the SAMPLES, not where they center. Twenty results stack into one mound, and the mound sits on the truth.
68 is next lesson's business — the share within one σ. The CENTER of the bell is the parameter itself: 50.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Samples overshoot and undershoot the truth in equal measure, so the mound centers on the parameter: 50.
widget.successFeedback: 50 — the bell is honest about its center: it stacks up right over the value the samples estimate.

steps.body: This mound has a name: the normal distribution. It appears whenever many small chances add up — sample proportions, measurement errors, heights. Same curve, different rulers: what changes is only its center (the mean) and its width (the standard deviation).

widget.prompt: A bell from samples of 10 vs a bell from samples of 50 — the difference?

options.label: Same shape; the 50-bell is narrower
options.feedback: Right — bigger samples wobble less, squeezing the bell.

options.label: The 50-bell becomes lopsided
options.feedback: Sample size changes spread, never symmetry.

options.label: They center on different values
options.feedback: Both center on the same truth — 0.5.

widget.successFeedback: Sample size tunes the WIDTH of the bell, not its center or symmetry. Tighter bell = steadier statistic.

explanationVariants: Averaging 50 instead of 10 gives chance more room to cancel itself, so the pile tightens; the center stays put.
Spread shrinks with sample size; symmetry and center are properties of honest sampling, not of n.

widget.prompt: A histogram of 1,000 die rolls (values 1–6): also a bell?

options.label: No — that one really is flat
options.feedback: Right: each face is equally likely. The bell belongs to AVERAGES and totals, not to single fair outcomes.

options.label: Yes — everything becomes a bell
options.feedback: Single rolls stay flat. Roll 50 dice and average them, though — the averages bell up.

options.label: No — it spikes at 3.5
options.feedback: 3.5 isn't even a face. Single rolls are uniform; means of many rolls are the ones that bell.

widget.successFeedback: The bell is the signature of accumulation — many small chances pooled. One fair pick is flat; averages of many picks mound up.

explanationVariants: A single fair die has six equally likely faces — a flat histogram. Only sums and averages of MANY chances build the bell.
The bell is the fingerprint of accumulation; one isolated random pick keeps whatever shape its own chances have.
hints: Ask what a histogram of SINGLE rolls looks like — is any face more likely than another?
Each face has probability 1/6, so 1,000 rolls pile roughly evenly on all six values.
Flat, not bell. The bell would appear only if you rolled many dice at once and plotted the AVERAGES.

steps.body: Stacked sample results form a symmetric mound — the normal distribution — centered on the truth, narrower for bigger samples. Next: the bell keeps a strict promise about how much lands within one, two, three widths.
takeaways: Stacked sample statistics form a symmetric mound — the normal distribution — with its peak on the truth.
Bigger samples narrow the bell; they never move its center or break its symmetry.
The bell belongs to accumulations (averages, totals) — single fair outcomes keep their own shapes.
steps.teaser: Next: the bell's strict promise — exactly how much lands within one, two, three widths.
